title: Confucius’s Rectification of Names — making titles and conduct answer to each other
when: Associated with Confucius (traditionally 551–479 BCE), the idea appears in Analects 13.3. The Analects is a layered text; scholars debate its formation and the passage’s precise date, so an exact year is not secure.
people: Confucius (Kongzi), his interlocutor Zilu, and later Confucian thinkers including Xunzi, whose theory of naming is related but distinct.
origin: Early Chinese thought in the Zhou-era states. The dialogue places the question in Wei, amid a disputed succession and competing claims to political titles.
idea: Asked what he would do first in governing Wei, Confucius answers zheng ming, often translated “rectifying” or “ordering names.” The passage traces a chain: when names and titles do not fit, speech cannot reliably guide action; public affairs, ritual order, and punishment falter, leaving people unsure how to act. Names are not just labels: social roles carry standards, and those who claim a title should make its obligations real. Yet scholars caution against treating this brief, textually debated passage as a complete Confucian philosophy of language. Both the meaning of zheng ming and its political application remain contested.
relevance: The idea invites scrutiny of public terms—“leader,” “expert,” “safe,” or “fair.” When institutions use them loosely, language can conceal responsibility and make rules arbitrary. Clear definitions matter, but justice also depends on whether conduct fulfills what words promise.
